540.title: Share what helps
540.hook: Lohicca thinks a good discovery should be kept to oneself; the Buddha disagrees
540.howItsDone: In Buddhist traditions, giving the teaching (dhamma-dana) is called the highest gift; teachers share it freely, and lay people support the printing and distribution of texts as an act of generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: viññana, and a monk who searched every heaven, pointed back to awareness itself. Your line: no footing. Today, a brahmin who thinks good things should be kept quiet.

You find something that really helps: a way to sleep better, a way through grief, a habit that calms you down. Do you tell people? Or do you think: everyone has to find their own way, what can one person do for another? The brahmin Lohicca, of the village of Salavatika, holds the second view, firmly. If a teacher discovers something good, he believes, they should keep it to themselves. Teaching others is just making new ties. So when he hears the Buddha is nearby, he sends his barber, Rosika, with a dinner invitation.
screen: `YOU FIND SOMETHING THAT HELPS.` → `KEEP IT TO YOURSELF?` → `LOHICCA SENDS HIS BARBER.`

segments.voice: On the way, the barber walks beside the Buddha and quietly asks a favor: please free my master from this view. At the meal, the Buddha asks Lohicca directly. Is it true you think this? Yes. So the Buddha asks about Lohicca's own life. You live off the revenue of Salavatika, granted by the king. Suppose someone said Lohicca should keep all of it for himself and share nothing with the people who depend on him. Would that person be helping those people, or endangering them? Endangering them, says Lohicca. Would that person have their welfare at heart? No. Then, the Buddha says, it's the same with your view. Someone who says a good discovery shouldn't be shared puts an obstacle in front of everyone who could have been helped by it. The Pali word underneath is anukampa, compassion: does such a person have others' welfare at heart? Keeping good things to yourself, he suggests, falls short of it. Then he adds a careful distinction. Some teachers deserve criticism: those who teach without having reached the goal themselves, and those whose students don't listen. And one teacher deserves none: someone who has truly found something good and shares it so that others reach it too. So sharing isn't preaching at everyone. It's not hoarding what genuinely helps. Lohicca's response is vivid. You've done for me, he says, what a man would do if he grabbed someone by the hair who was falling off a cliff, and set them on solid ground.
screen: `THE BARBER ASKS A FAVOR` · `WOULD YOU HOARD SALAVATIKA'S REVENUE?` · `ANUKAMPA: COMPASSION` · `PULLED BACK FROM THE CLIFF` · then, large: `SHARE WHAT HELPS.`

segments.voice: Think of something that has truly helped you, not something to sell anyone on: a practice, a book, a kindness, a way of seeing. Bring to mind one person who might need it, picture telling them simply, with no pressure, and let a little warmth toward them rise.
Anukampa. A good discovery kept to yourself is a gift withheld; shared with compassion, it can pull someone back from the edge. Today's word.
Your line: set them on solid ground. What helped you can help someone else. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 540 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LINE OF THE BLIND.`

541.title: The line of the blind
541.hook: brahmins who've never seen Brahma are a line of blind men, each holding the one in front
541.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many schools encourage students to test teachings against their own experience, citing discourses like DN 13 and the Kalama Sutta, while still valuing lineage and the guidance of experienced teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anukampa, and Lohicca pulled back from the cliff. Your line: set them on solid ground. Today, two young men arguing on a walk.

Two young brahmins, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, are out walking near a village in Kosala, stretching their legs, and arguing. The question is a serious one in their world: which path leads to union with Brahma? Each says it's the path his own teacher teaches. Neither can convince the other. Then they remember that the Buddha is staying nearby, in a mango grove by the river Aciravati. Let's ask him. That conversation is the thirteenth long discourse.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ARGUING ON A WALK.` → `WHICH PATH LEADS TO BRAHMA?` → `LET'S ASK HIM.`

segments.voice: Vasettha puts it generously. All these teachers' paths, he says, maybe they're like the many roads near a village: different routes, all arriving at the same place. The Buddha doesn't argue with the picture. He asks about the evidence. Vasettha, has any of the brahmins who know the three Vedas seen Brahma face to face? No. Their teachers? No. Their teachers' teachers, back seven generations? No. The ancient sages who composed the verses, did they ever say: we know where Brahma is, we have seen him? No. Then, the Buddha says, it's like a line of blind men, each holding on to the one in front. The first one doesn't see. The one in the middle doesn't see. The last one doesn't see. The Pali is andhaveni: a line, a braid, of the blind. Two things are worth holding carefully here. First, this is a conversation in its own time, between the Buddha and two students, about the specific claims of their teachers. Hindu traditions today understand Brahma, Brahman and the Vedas in many ways, and this text isn't a verdict on them. Second, the image cuts for everyone, Buddhists included. Any teaching passed hand to hand, by people who trust the person in front, can become a line of the blind. The Buddha's question works as a test. Has anyone in the chain actually seen? Can you see for yourself? And he doesn't stop at criticism. The conversation goes on, and tomorrow he describes a path the young men can walk and check for themselves.
screen: `MANY ROADS TO ONE VILLAGE?` · `HAS ANYONE SEEN BRAHMA?` · `EACH HOLDING THE ONE IN FRONT` · `THE IMAGE CUTS FOR EVERYONE` · then, large: `THE LINE OF THE BLIND.`

segments.voice: Choose something you were taught and never checked, about money, people or yourself, and picture the line it came down: from whom, and from whom before that. Then ask the Buddha's question: has anyone in this line actually seen it, and have I? You don't have to throw it away; just hold it as untested for now, and breathe.
Andhaveni. A teaching passed hand to hand, each trusting the one in front, with no one who has seen for themselves. Today's word.
Your line: can you see for yourself? The question works on every chain, your own included. That's day five hundred forty-one.

542.title: Like a trumpeter
542.hook: the four immeasurables sounded in every direction, like a strong trumpeter
542.howItsDone: In many Buddhist traditions people practice the four brahmaviharas by sending loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity outward in each direction in turn, often as part of a daily sit or a chanted metta practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: andhaveni, the line of the blind. Your line: can you see for yourself? Today the same discourse turns around and offers a way forward.

Long before loudspeakers, a strong player could lift a conch shell and send one clear note out over the fields. He doesn't aim it. He doesn't send it down one road. The sound simply goes out, and nobody within reach is left out of hearing it. The Pali word for him is sankhadhama: a conch-blower. That is the picture the Buddha reaches for near the end of the Tevijja Sutta, the thirteenth of the Long Discourses. Yesterday he took apart a claim. Today he hands the young brahmin Vasettha something to do instead.
screen: `A CONCH-BLOWER'S NOTE.` → `IT GOES EVERYWHERE AT ONCE.` → `THE END OF DN 13.`

segments.voice: Vasettha and his friend wanted the straight road to union with Brahma, the high god of their teachers. The Buddha has just shown that their teachers never saw Brahma. But he doesn't walk away. He asks: is Brahma, as you describe him, full of hate or free of it? Free of it, they say. Burdened with possessions or free of them? Free. Then he describes a monk who becomes like that. First, the monk lets go of the five hindrances, and gladness rises. Then he lets a mind of loving-kindness fill one direction, then the second, the third, the fourth, then above, below, around, everywhere: a mind wide, grown great, without measure, free of hate. Then the same with compassion. Then with gladness at others' joy. Then with equanimity. Elsewhere the texts call these four the brahmaviharas, the dwellings of Brahma; they're also called the four immeasurables. And here's the image. As a strong trumpeter makes himself heard in all four directions without any strain, so this mind leaves out no living thing. It doesn't choose who gets to hear. Here is the move. The Buddha takes the brahmins' own goal, union with Brahma, and gives it content. Not a place you travel to by argument, but a heart you grow, one direction at a time. In a number of Buddhist communities the four are still practiced this way, radiating outward, direction by direction. And the image carries one more detail: the conch-blower is heard with little difficulty. The note isn't forced.

Brahmavihara. The four immeasurables from the Tevijja Sutta: a mind of goodwill heard in every direction, leaving no one out, without strain. Today's word.
Your line: the note isn't forced. A heart grown wide reaches everyone without strain. Rest well.

543.title: Vipassi's four sights
543.hook: the story of a past Buddha, Vipassi, who also saw the four sights
543.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor seven Buddhas of the past, from Vipassi to Gotama, in chants such as the Atanatiya verses, and the four sights are retold in temples, festivals and art across the Buddhist world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: brahmavihara, a mind of goodwill heard in every direction. Your line: the note isn't forced. Today, a story you may think you already know, told about someone else.

A prince rides out of the palace to the royal park. On the road his charioteer slows down. There's a man by the road, bent over, gray, leaning on a stick. What's wrong with him? the prince asks. He's old, the charioteer says. Will I get old? Everyone does, sir. The prince turns the chariot around and goes home, shaken. Most people know this scene as the young Siddhattha's. But in the oldest detailed telling in the Pali canon, the prince in the chariot has a different name.
screen: `AN OLD MAN BY THE ROAD.` → `WILL I GET OLD?` → `A DIFFERENT PRINCE.`

segments.voice: The fourteenth Long Discourse, the Mahapadana, the great story, begins with monks chatting about past lives. The Buddha joins them and names six Buddhas before himself, going back ninety-one aeons to the first, Vipassi. Then he tells Vipassi's life in full. Vipassi's father, King Bandhuma, hears a prediction that his son will either rule the world or leave it. So he surrounds him with pleasures. Then, on four separate trips to the park, Vipassi sees an old man, then a sick man, then a dead man carried out with mourners. Each time he turns back troubled, and each time his father adds more pleasures. On the fourth trip he sees a shaven-headed wanderer in a robe. What is he? A man who has gone forth, sir, who lives kindly and harmlessly. Vipassi goes forth. Alone, he reflects: this world has fallen into trouble. It's born, it ages, it dies. How does anyone escape? He traces the conditions back, link by link, and awakens. Even his hesitation to teach is there, and a Brahma who asks him to. The sutta calls this kind of pattern dhammata, the way things are for every Buddha. In the canon, the four sights are told in detail of Vipassi; later biographies tell the same scene of Gotama, the Buddha of our age. Why tell it this way? Because the point isn't one remarkable prince. Whenever anyone looks clearly at aging, sickness and death, the same questions rise. It happens again.

segments.voice: Let four faces come, one at a time: someone old you know, someone who is sick or was, someone who has died, and don't hurry past any of them. Then a fourth: someone calm, who has made peace with some of this, and rest with that face. The questions Vipassi asked are yours to ask too, if you want them.
Vipassi, the first Buddha named in the Mahapadana Sutta, who saw age, sickness, death and a wanderer, a pattern later told of Gotama too. Today's word.
Your line: it happens again. People have stood exactly here before, asking the same questions. Day five hundred forty-three, done.

544.title: "Don't say that, Ananda"
544.hook: Ananda finds dependent origination clear; the Buddha says it is deep
544.howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist schools return to dependent origination again and again over years of study, and the Mahanidana Sutta is often studied slowly, link by link, in monastic and lay study groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vipassi's four sights. Your line: it happens again. Today, the Buddha's attendant says something a little too confident.

A flat-pack bookshelf comes with one page of instructions. Read once, it looks simple. An hour later, someone is sitting on the floor surrounded by screws. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, has heard the teaching again and again. One day in the market town of Kammasadhamma he comes to the Buddha and says, in effect: it's wonderful how deep this teaching of dependent origination is, and yet to me it seems perfectly clear. The answer he gets opens the fifteenth Long Discourse.
screen: `THAT LOOKS SIMPLE.` → `ANANDA: DEEP, BUT CLEAR TO ME.` → `THE BUDDHA ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Mahanidana, the great discourse on causes. The Buddha's reply comes twice: don't say that, Ananda, don't say that. This dependent origination is deep, and it looks deep. It is because people don't understand it, don't penetrate it, that this generation has become like a tangled ball of thread, like a knotted skein, like matted reeds and rushes, and can't get past the round of birth and death. He doesn't call Ananda stupid. The warning is aimed at one particular mistake: confusing familiar with understood. Then, instead of arguing, the Buddha teaches it again, slowly, from the other end. Aging and death have a condition: birth. Birth has a condition: becoming. And on back through clinging, craving, feeling and contact, until he reaches a strange loop. Consciousness depends on name-and-form, and name-and-form depends on consciousness, like two sheaves of reeds leaning on each other, to borrow an image from another sutta. He even walks through craving in the world: because of craving, seeking; because of seeking, gain; and on down to the stick and the knife, quarrels and lies. One teaching, from the deepest roots of a life to an argument at a family dinner. Tradition remembers Ananda as the one who carried the discourses home in memory. And here, the one who had heard so much is told: slow down. It is deeper than it looks.

Your line: deeper than it looks. Familiar is not the same as understood. See you tomorrow.

545.title: Seven conditions of welfare
545.hook: the last journey begins: a people thrives while it meets often and in harmony
545.howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities meet regularly, most visibly at the fortnightly uposatha gathering where the monastic rules are recited, and many lay groups keep weekly sittings and study meetings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: paticcasamuppada, a teaching that looked clear and wasn't. Your line: deeper than it looks. Today the discourse of the Buddha's last journey begins, and the path walks it for a week.

A king wants a war. Ajatasattu of Magadha, the same king who rode out on a moonlit night a few weeks back on this path, has decided to crush the Vajjians, a confederation of clans to the north. Before he marches, he sends his chief minister, Vassakara, to the Buddha on Vulture's Peak, with orders: tell him my plan, and bring back exactly what he says. For, the king says, a Buddha does not speak falsely. So the minister arrives, bows, and lays out the plan. And the Buddha doesn't answer him. He turns to Ananda, who is standing behind him, fanning him.
screen: `A KING WANTS A WAR.` → `THE MINISTER ON VULTURE'S PEAK.` → `THE BUDDHA TURNS TO ANANDA.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the great discourse on the final passing, the account of the Buddha's last months. Maha means great. Parinibbana is the complete going out, the death of one already awakened. It begins, of all places, with politics. Ananda, the Buddha asks, have you heard that the Vajjians meet often, and in large numbers? I have, sir. Then, as long as they do, they can be expected to grow, not decline. And he goes through seven questions. Do they meet in harmony, rise in harmony, and do their business in harmony? Do they keep their established laws, neither making new ones nor throwing out the old? Do they honor and listen to their elders? Do they refrain from carrying off women and girls by force? Do they honor their shrines? Do they protect those who live the holy life among them? Seven yeses, seven reasons to thrive. The minister gets the message. The Vajjians, he says, can't be beaten in war, only by diplomacy or by splitting them apart. And he goes. Then the Buddha calls the monks together and gives them seven conditions of their own, starting the same way: as long as you meet often, and in harmony, you can be expected to grow, not decline. Look at what comes first. Not doctrine. Not meditation. Meeting. People who keep showing up, and who leave on good terms. The Buddha's great final journey opens with a lesson about how communities stay alive.

segments.voice: Call to mind the people you belong with, a family, a team, friends, a congregation, and picture the last time you were all together. Let one face come up whom you haven't seen in a while, breathe with it, and hold one wish for the group: may we keep meeting, in harmony.
Mahaparinibbana. The great final passing, the name of the Long Discourse that tells the Buddha's last journey. Today's word.
Your line: meet often, in harmony. Showing up, and leaving on good terms, comes first. That's day five hundred forty-five.

546.title: Ambapali's invitation
546.hook: the courtesan invites the Buddha to a meal; he keeps his word even when princes ask later
546.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics traditionally accept a meal invitation by silence and keep it once accepted, and lay families across Asia still invite monks to their homes for a meal offering, often to mark a birthday or a memorial.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahaparinibbana, and the last journey began. Your line: meet often, in harmony. Today closes a week, and on the road north the Buddha gets two invitations for the same meal.

Two chariots race side by side on the road out of Vesali, wheel against wheel, axle against axle. In one, a woman. In the others, a crowd of young nobles in bright clothes, furious. She's just come from the Buddha, who is staying in her own mango grove. She invited him and his monks to a meal tomorrow, and he accepted, by staying silent, which is how he says yes. The nobles are on their way to invite him to the very same meal. They shout: give it to us, and we'll pay you a hundred thousand.
screen: `TWO CHARIOTS, AXLE TO AXLE.` → `SHE ASKED FIRST.` → `A HUNDRED THOUSAND FOR THE MEAL.`

segments.voice: Ambapali was a courtesan of Vesali, and the Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells her part simply. Her answer to the nobles: even if you gave me Vesali and all its lands, I wouldn't give up that meal. The young men snap their fingers: we've been beaten by the mango woman. Then they drive on to the Buddha anyway and invite him for tomorrow. He tells them he has already accepted Ambapali's invitation. That's all. No speech about status, no lecture about her work. The first invitation stands. The next day, in her own house, Ambapali serves the Buddha and the monks with her own hands. And when the meal is over, she gives her mango grove to the community. The text records the gift plainly, with no comment on who she was. The Elders' Verses of the nuns, the Therigatha, remember her later as a nun herself, with verses on her own aging body attributed to her. Look back at this week. Lohicca, set them on solid ground. The line of the blind: can you see for yourself? The trumpeter whose note isn't forced. Vipassi's four sights. Ananda told, don't say that. The Vajjians who meet in harmony. And now a promise kept, to the person who asked first, whoever she was.
screen: `NOT FOR ALL OF VESALI.` · `BEATEN BY THE MANGO WOMAN.` · `HE HAD ALREADY SAID YES.` · `THE GROVE GIVEN.` · then, large: `FIRST COME, FIRST HONORED.`

segments.voice: Think of a small promise you've already made, a call, a visit, a meal, and picture a better offer arriving for the same time. Notice whether it pulls, without judging it. Then feel what it would be like to keep the first one anyway.
Ambapali's invitation. The courtesan of Vesali who asked the Buddha first; he kept his word when the nobles asked later, and she gave her grove. Today's word.
Your line: first come, first honored. A promise kept, to whoever asked first. A week, done.
